title: Bengal's industrial policy: land bank, no forced acquisition, power and EPF incentives
dek: Chief Minister Suvendu Adhikari unveiled the Investment Promotion Policy, 2026, saying the state will buy land from willing owners for a land bank and pool plots with farmers, while facing a Rs 50,000 crore backlog of unpaid incentives.
author: Declaration Desk
body:
Chief Minister Suvendu Adhikari on Thursday unveiled West Bengal's Investment Promotion Policy, 2026, the BJP government's first full industrial policy, and set out how it plans to find land for factories in a state where the issue has toppled governments. The state will buy land from willing owners to build a land bank, pool plots with farmers' participation, and use the 2013 central land acquisition law, he said, but will not take land by force.

The policy pairs that land plan with a menu of incentives: help with investment in plant and machinery, a share of employers' provident fund contributions, electricity tariff relief for up to five years, and fixed deadlines for approvals through a single-window portal. Adhikari said the state could facilitate about Rs 1 lakh crore of fresh investment "over the coming months", according to a PTI report carried by Millennium Post.

## What happened

Adhikari presented the policy at a press conference in Kolkata on Thursday afternoon. The state cabinet had cleared a draft on 28 October; the Chief Minister said then that the government had taken time to "fine tune it" after seeking every minister's views, UNI reported.

On land, he drew a line against both previous governments. "We will neither have a forcible land acquisition policy like the Left Front, nor will we have a flawed land policy like the TMC," he said, according to PTI. "We cannot go back to the days when farmers were fired upon for land acquisition." The Trinamool Congress government's approach, under which companies had to buy their own land, was blamed by Adhikari for 15 years of weak industrial growth.

Under the new route, the state will first buy land directly from owners and hold it in a land bank, then allot it to projects, IANS reported. Other plots will come from existing industrial parks and from encroached land the state has recovered. ETV Bharat reported that he named both the Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act, 2013 and a "land pooling" model that relies on "the active participation of the original landowners". The government is talking to HUDCO, NABARD, the Asian Development Bank and other lenders about financing land purchases, and is studying the land policies of Uttar Pradesh, Maharashtra, Gujarat and Andhra Pradesh, PTI reported.

Companies that hold land allotted by the previous government but have not used it must start their projects within three months or return the plots for a refund of the original price, he said.

## What the policy offers

The full policy document had not been published on a state government website by Thursday evening, so the details below are as reported by news agencies; figures may change when the notification is issued.

- Plant and machinery: assistance of up to 100% of the investment for general units, 110% for "thrust" sectors and 120% for "priority" sectors, paid in instalments after production begins (IANS)
- Provident fund: the state will pay the employer's share of EPF for women and transgender employees in MSMEs in full, and half for men, for up to 10 years (IANS); large units employing at least 200 people in priority areas, or 400 elsewhere, get 50% for five years, capped at Rs 10 crore (KNN India)
- Power: exemption from electricity tariff for up to five years for new manufacturing and services investments (IANS)
- Research: 50% of the cost of R&D facilities, or 75% for fully export-oriented units, up to Rs 5 crore (KNN India)
- Approvals: a certificate of intent within 30 days and a certificate of eligibility within 45 days of starting production, through a single-window portal (IANS)
- Mega projects: help with roads, water and power connections, tied to creating 50 jobs per acre (IANS)

Thrust sectors listed in the draft include semiconductors, electronics, green hydrogen, electric vehicles and batteries, defence, shipbuilding, food processing and textiles, KNN India reported, citing The Indian Express. Sponge iron plants, traditional brick kilns, asbestos products, banned single-use plastics, firecracker manufacturing and most thermal power plants are excluded from incentives.

## Background

The BJP formed its first government in Bengal in May 2026. Its first budget, presented on 22 June, set aside Rs 5,000 crore to promote industry, and Finance Minister Swapan Dasgupta had promised an incentive policy before Durga Puja. That deadline slipped; Adhikari later said the policy would come after Diwali.

Land has shaped Bengal politics for two decades. Protests against land acquisition for the Tata Nano car plant at Singur, led by the Trinamool Congress, ended with Tata Motors leaving the state in 2008. Police firing at Nandigram in 2007, during protests against a proposed chemical hub, killed 14 people. Both episodes helped end 34 years of Left Front rule in 2011. Asked about Singur on Thursday, Adhikari said his government had held preliminary talks with Ashok Leyland, The Statesman reported.

The new government also inherits a large bill. Adhikari said unpaid incentives promised to companies under earlier schemes add up to about Rs 50,000 crore, which he said was beyond the state's current means. His government will honour commitments that fell due after 9 May 2026 and deal with the older dues "once the state is financially stronger", PTI reported.

## What they are saying

Adhikari said land had already been handed to 33 business groups in his government's first six months, and named projects by Amul, Vedanta, Reliance, the Sanjiv Goenka group and JSW. "We have a zero-tolerance policy towards any form of extortion from industry," he said. He accused the Left of damaging industry through "aggressive" trade unionism and alleged that about Rs 20,000 crore of state revenue had been siphoned off under the TMC; he did not give evidence for the figure in the reports seen by The Declaration.

Kolkata economist Probir Mukherjee told IANS that because land holdings in Bengal are "extremely fragmented", large investments are unlikely without the state's help in assembling land, but that forced acquisition can backfire, as Singur and Nandigram showed.

No response from the Trinamool Congress or the CPI(M) to Thursday's policy had been reported by the time of publication.

## What happens next

The government is expected to notify the policy and open the single-window portal; the reports did not give a date. Land-pooling will need rules, and possibly amendments to state land laws. Investors will be watching whether the land bank is funded, how quickly the state clears its incentive backlog, and whether the Rs 1 lakh crore figure turns into signed projects. JSW chairman Sajjan Jindal has proposed laying the foundation stone for the second phase of the Salboni power plant in January, Adhikari said.
